issues.problem: Target proof trusts unreviewed working-tree state: only age recipients are required to match HEAD; cookwright.json and the 1Password template are not checked as tracked and HEAD-identical.
issues.suggested_fix: Before a proved run, require cookwright.json and any 1Password template to be tracked and byte-identical to HEAD; refuse before resolution otherwise. Test modifying each after commit, asserting exit 125 and no child spawned.
issues.failure_scenario: An uncommitted edit changes dev's ref/template/ciphertext to production; `cookwright run dev` proves production values against the relabelled ref and spawns the command under a dev banner.
issues.evidence: Disposition 49 (§4.2 step 5, step 6 banner): run now names every uncommitted path among cookwright.json, the template and the ciphertext on the banner from one `git status --porcelain --` (top-relative per disposition 54), tested per file, so a relabelled target is no longer spawned silently under a plain dev banner. Not refusing is a reasoned rule-2/3 choice (the setup recipe runs before committing), not an omission.

issues.problem: Secret-bearing helper processes and backend credentials cross the environment boundary: age/security calls omit env so inherit stale declared and ambient secrets; the final child inherits 1Password auth variables (OP_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_TOKEN, OP_SESSION_*).
issues.suggested_fix: Define separate resolver and child environments. Strip declared/ambient secrets from every helper; additionally drop backend-control credentials (including dynamic OP_SESSION_*) from the final child. Test the exact env received by each helper and the child.
issues.failure_scenario: A stale production DB_URL is passed to age/security, or an app run via the 1Password backend receives a service-account token able to read the vault.
issues.evidence: Disposition 50, disposition 9 ('Every helper runs with the scrubbed environment'), §4.2 steps 3 and 5, §4.1 controlNames: helpers get declared, ambient and value-equal names removed; the child additionally loses OP_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_TOKEN, OP_CONNECT_*, every OP_SESSION_* and COOKWRIGHT_AGE_IDENTITY; §6 engine tests assert each helper's and the child's exact environment, OP_SESSION_x included.

issues.problem: Identity-location check uses underWorkTree(path, repo.top) so it does not detect an identity inside a different repo (dotfiles symlink) despite claiming to; POSIX permission policy is mentioned but never defined.
issues.suggested_fix: Detect any enclosing Git work tree of the resolved identity path, refuse before writing. Define and test a POSIX mode policy, FAIL on group/world-readable plaintext identities.
issues.failure_scenario: ~/.config symlinks into ~/dotfiles; init writes the identity into another Git repo; a pre-existing 0644 passphrase-less identity escapes detection.
issues.evidence: The POSIX policy is now defined (disposition 51: identity 0600, directory 0700, doctor FAILs group/world-readable) and the check widened to any work tree, but a residual holds. Disposition 51 and §4.3 age.mjs init still decide by `git -C <dir> rev-parse --show-toplevel` exits 0 on the realpath of the identity's directory, and init runs that preflight before its own `mkdir -p` (§4.3: preflight 'identity absent and outside every work tree', then 'mkdir -p mode 700'). On a first init $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/cookwright (or a COOKWRIGHT_AGE_IDENTITY parent) usually does not exist yet: realpath throws and git -C exits 128, so a non-zero exit reads as 'outside every work tree' and the identity is written into the dotfiles repo (or a not-yet-created dir inside this repo). Doctor FAILs it afterwards, but init does not refuse. The plan should judge the nearest existing ancestor (or the realpath of the parent chain) and test the absent-directory case.

issues.problem: Default keychain service cookwright/<basename>/<target> is not per repository; same-basename repos collide and -U can overwrite the other's item.
issues.suggested_fix: Require an explicit stable secrets.id for the keychain backend or generate a unique non-secret id at setup. Test two repos with the same basename.
issues.failure_scenario: /client-a/app and /client-b/app both use target prod; setting a key in one overwrites or retrieves the other's item.
issues.evidence: Disposition 52 and §4.1: no basename default; secrets.id is required by the config when backend is keychain, service cookwright/<id>/<target>; §6 tests two repos with the same basename and different ids. Disposition 26 updated accordingly.

The 'any byte but newline' claim is gone from disposition 15.

issues.problem: Redactor transport can corrupt/truncate child output: StringDecoder is text-only and replaces invalid UTF-8; backpressure unspecified; ending after arbitrary 200 ms can discard buffered output.
issues.suggested_fix: Use a byte-safe transform with normal backpressure and wait for both pipes to close, or explicitly narrow the contract to text. Test invalid UTF-8, large output via slow consumer, delayed post-exit data.
issues.failure_scenario: `run ... -- pg_dump -Fc > dump` yields a corrupt/truncated dump; high-volume child grows memory.
issues.evidence: Disposition 59 and §4.5: byte Redactor (Buffer needles, Buffer.indexOf, byte hold-back), a Transform piped with normal backpressure, run exits only after both pipes closed and the child exited (200 ms drain removed); §6 tests invalid UTF-8 untouched, binary byte-identical, a slow consumer with large output, a grandchild holding the pipe.

issues.problem: The 'one child' residual omits descendants, which inherit the env; plan recommends sh -c wrappers and acknowledges grandchildren elsewhere.

issues.problem: The keychain write path relies on `security add-generic-password ... -w` (last) prompting for the value. Measured on this machine: /usr/bin/security links `_getpass` (nm -u) and its prompt strings are 'password data for new item:' and 'retype password for new item:'. getpass(3) on macOS says 'The password may be up to _PASSWORD_LEN (currently 128) characters ... Any additional characters ... are discarded' (pwd.h: `#define _PASSWORD_LEN 128`). Both prompts truncate the same way, so the retype matches and nothing reports an error. `find-generic-password -w` also prints hex for a non-ASCII value, so that value is injected hex-encoded.
issues.suggested_fix: Before s3, measure a 200+ character value round-tripped through the prompt. If it truncates, take this back to the developer, because it contradicts their dated decision 48. One candidate keeps the value off any command line: `security -i`, which reads the `add-generic-password ... -w <value>` command from stdin. Its quoting and length limits need measuring too. Whatever path is chosen, check after every set that the stored length matches the input length (compare the sha256), and refuse otherwise. Add a test with a 220-character value and a non-ASCII value, and a QA step with a real service-role JWT.
issues.failure_scenario: The developer runs `secrets set dev SERVICE_ROLE_KEY` on the keychain backend and pastes a Supabase service-role JWT (about 220 characters), or a pooler DB_URL longer than 128 characters. security keeps the first 128 characters and exits 0, and cookwright prints 'set SERVICE_ROLE_KEY'. Every later `run dev` injects the truncated key and the proof still passes (it does not cover that name). Calls then fail with opaque auth errors, and nothing in doctor or run points at the cause.
issues.evidence: Disposition 60, §4.3 keychain.mjs set, §6, §8, §12: the prompt-through-security mechanism is dropped; cookwright's own echo-off prompt then `security -i` fed the add line on stdin, measured in s3 (220-character, spaces/quotes, non-ASCII) before building, a read-back sha256 check after every set refusing on mismatch, and a refusal path if security -i fails; the contradiction with decision 48 is taken to the developer in §12.

issues.problem: The child's stdout and stderr always go through a Redactor that decodes the bytes as UTF-8 text with a StringDecoder and writes strings back out. Any byte sequence that is not valid UTF-8 is replaced with U+FFFD (EF BF BD), whether or not a needle matched. So `run` silently corrupts every binary stream a child writes, and the plan's tests (§6, redactor: multibyte split only) never cover binary output.
issues.suggested_fix: Redact on Buffers: hold the needles as Buffers (both the raw and the encoded forms) and search with Buffer.indexOf. Keep the same prefix hold-back on bytes, and pass bytes through unchanged when nothing matches. Add a redactor test and an engine test that pipe random binary (and a pg_dump-shaped header) through and assert the bytes are identical.
issues.failure_scenario: `npx cookwright run prod -- pg_dump -Fc > backup.dump` (or `-- tar c ...`, `-- gzip -c`): cookwright's stdout is the file, and the child's binary stdout passes through the StringDecoder. Each invalid UTF-8 sequence becomes EF BF BD, the command exits 0, and the file is a corrupted backup that is only found when `pg_restore` fails later.
issues.evidence: Disposition 59 and §4.5: the redactor works on Buffers and passes bytes unchanged when nothing matches; §6 engine and redactor tests and §8 fixture (`head -c 4096 /dev/urandom | cmp`) assert binary output byte-identical.

issues.location: dispositions 11 and 29, §8 fixture second doctor run, §10 s3 'the fixture green'
issues.problem: `secrets.carriers` reads doctor's own environment and the real `~/.zshrc` and similar files for every ambient name of the declared packs. The fixture declares `supabase`, and isolate_git does not isolate HOME or the environment. Measured on this machine (names only): `~/.zshrc` has `export SUPABASE_DB_URL=`, and `SUPABASE_DB_URL` is set in the environment. That name is on the supabase pack's ambient list (disposition 29). The fixture's first doctor run asserts ' 0 FAIL, 1 WARN, ' (or ' 0 FAIL, 0 WARN, '), and the second asserts `PASS secrets.carriers` and exact counts.

Alternatively, make the carriers assertion depend on the environment. Add an assertion that a planted rc line WARNs, so the row is measured rather than assumed.

The first doctor run shows 2 WARN and fails 'doctor reported a FAIL, or a WARN besides pack.supabase.types'. The plan's 'fixture green at the end of every session' is false locally even though the ubuntu CI job passes.

issues.problem: skills.test.mjs 'acts on every PASS row of its recipe at the end' requires the note of every `| PASS |` recipe row to appear in the text after `## At the end`. issues.location: §4.1 validateSecrets ('`targets` a non-empty object') vs disposition 44; s1 disposition list

Disposition 34 (Refused, 'exit 1') also contradicts 47 (125). The config is invalid, so `config` FAILs and every config-dependent row SKIPs, which is the state amendment 44 forbids. s3 then has to rewrite s1's validator and tests.

issues.problem: The proofs check only the URL's authority (the pooler username and the host). libpq connection URIs accept the connection parameters in the query string as well, and those override the authority: `?host=`, `?hostaddr=`, `?user=`, `?service=`, `?port=`. The near-miss table only covers the expected ref appearing in the query (unanchored), never a query parameter that redirects the connection. The `host` kind has the same gap. A supabase-proved banner then claims more than the check establishes.
issues.suggested_fix: For postgres-scheme values, refuse as a mismatch any query parameter in {host, hostaddr, user, service, port, dbname, options}, or refuse any query that libpq would read as a connection parameter, naming the parameter but never the value. Add `?user=postgres.<other>`, `?host=db.<other>.supabase.co` and `?hostaddr=` rows to the near-miss table, in both kinds.
issues.failure_scenario: dev's DB_URL is `postgresql://postgres.<devref>:pw@aws-0-eu.pooler.supabase.com:6543/postgres?user=postgres.<prodref>`, for example a pasted connection string with an edited query. The proof sees username `postgres.<devref>` on a pooler host and prints 'proved DB_URL against <devref>'. psql connects as `postgres.<prodref>`, and the pooler routes to prod: the stale-target incident the proof exists to stop.
issues.evidence: Disposition 65, disposition 19, §4.4 pgQueryProblem shared by both kinds: a postgres-scheme value with host, hostaddr, user, port, dbname, service, options, password or passfile in the query (percent-decoded names) is a mismatch naming the parameter only; §6 near-miss table gains ?user=, ?host=, ?hostaddr=, ?pass%77ord=, and host-kind `?host=`.

issues.location: disposition 6 ('a symlinked `~/.config` into a dotfiles repo counts'), §4.3 age.mjs `underWorkTree`
issues.problem: The identity check compares the realpath of the identity's directory against this repo's work tree only. A `~/.config` symlinked into a dotfiles repository resolves into a different work tree, so the check passes it, yet the parenthetical says that case 'counts'. The claim is wider than the check. Dotfiles repos are often pushed publicly, and the `--no-passphrase` identity is a plaintext AGE-SECRET-KEY. gitleaks only scans this repo's commits.
issues.suggested_fix: Refuse (init) or FAIL (doctor) when the identity's realpath directory is inside any git work tree: `git -C <dir> rev-parse --is-inside-work-tree` exits 0. Name that repo's top, not only this one. Add a test with a symlinked config dir pointing into a second scratch repo.
issues.failure_scenario: The developer's ~/.config is a symlink to ~/dotfiles/config, a public GitHub repo. `secrets init --no-passphrase` writes ~/.config/cookwright/identity.age, whose realpath ~/dotfiles/config/cookwright is not under the app's work tree, so init accepts it and doctor does not FAIL. The next `git add -A && git push` in dotfiles publishes the key that decrypts every tracked `secrets/*.env.age`.
issues.evidence: Disposition 51 now refuses any enclosing work tree naming its top and adds a symlinked-config test, but the mechanism misses the very first init. Disposition 51 and §4.3 age.mjs init still decide by `git -C <dir> rev-parse --show-toplevel` exits 0 on the realpath of the identity's directory, and init runs that preflight before its own `mkdir -p` (§4.3: preflight 'identity absent and outside every work tree', then 'mkdir -p mode 700'). On a first init $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/cookwright (or a COOKWRIGHT_AGE_IDENTITY parent) usually does not exist yet: realpath throws and git -C exits 128, so a non-zero exit reads as 'outside every work tree' and the identity is written into the dotfiles repo (or a not-yet-created dir inside this repo). Doctor FAILs it afterwards, but init does not refuse. The plan should judge the nearest existing ancestor (or the realpath of the parent chain) and test the absent-directory case.

issues.location: disposition 13 ('cookwright ignores SIGINT and SIGTERM while the child runs'), §4.2 step 7
issues.problem: Ignoring SIGINT is right for a terminal, which signals the whole foreground group. SIGTERM, though, normally comes from a supervisor that signals one pid: a wrapper's `child.kill()`, a CI step timeout, an agent host killing a stuck command, or `kill <pid>`. With SIGTERM ignored and not forwarded, cookwright neither exits nor passes the signal on, so the child is never told to stop. §6 tests only 'SIGINT ignored while the child runs'.
issues.suggested_fix: Forward SIGTERM and SIGHUP to the child (`child.kill(sig)`) and keep waiting. Exit with 128+n from the child's own end, and keep SIGINT ignored, since the terminal already delivers it to the child. Add an engine test that sends SIGTERM to the cookwright process alone and asserts the child receives it and the exit is 143.
issues.failure_scenario: An orchestrator or wrapper times out `npx cookwright run dev -- node long-migration.js` and sends SIGTERM to cookwright's pid. cookwright ignores it, and the migration keeps running against the database with nothing told to stop it. The wrapper escalates to SIGKILL, which kills cookwright and orphans the child. The child keeps running with the injected secrets in its environment, and its output is now written to a closed pipe.
issues.evidence: Disposition 66, disposition 13: SIGINT ignored, SIGTERM and SIGHUP forwarded with child.kill(signal), cookwright keeps waiting, exit 128+n; §6 tests SIGTERM sent to cookwright alone reaches the child, exit 143.

issues.location: dispositions 9 and 40, §4.7 managed block ('a command that needs a credential runs through `{{cli}} run <target> -- …`')
issues.problem: The block tells the agent to run credentialed commands through `run`. With the charter's recommended free path, `age` with a passphrase-protected identity, `run` refuses whenever there is no terminal (disposition 40), and an agent's tool shell has none. No cache along the lines of ssh-agent exists, so with the recommended setup the agent can never use `run`. The only states in which an agent can use the age backend are the WARN state (`--no-passphrase`) and the other two backends. Neither the block nor the guide says this, and the refusal's remedy, 'run in a terminal', gives an agent nothing to do.
issues.suggested_fix: State the limit in the block, the guide and the setup recipe: with a passphrase-protected age identity, `run` is the developer's command, and the agent asks the developer to run it. Make the refusal line say exactly that (for example, 'hand this command to the developer'). It must never point at `--no-passphrase`. Alternatively, log an unlock-cache enhancement in the backlog.
issues.failure_scenario: A user follows the setup skill: `age`, a passphrase identity, the PASS path. In the next session the agent, obeying the block, runs `npx cookwright run dev -- supabase db push` and gets exit 125, 'the identity is passphrase-protected; run in a terminal'. It retries or improvises, for example suggesting `secrets init --no-passphrase` to 'fix' it, which downgrades the user's security to get past a refusal the plan treats as working as intended.
issues.evidence: Disposition 67, §4.7 block and setup recipe: with a passphrase-protected age identity the run command is the developer's (block line), the no-terminal refusal reads 'hand this command to the developer' and never names --no-passphrase; an unlock cache is a backlog entry (§9).

issues.problem: The whole value of every declared name, and the inherited value of every declared or ambient name, becomes a substring needle for both the argv check and the redactor, with no minimum length. The ambient list includes names that hold non-secret, often short values (`PGSERVICE`, `PGSERVICEFILE`, `PGPASSFILE`). A declared low-entropy value (a mode, a port, a public URL) likewise becomes a needle. Disposition 14 also drops any inherited variable whose value equals a resolved value. §11 notes only the redaction cost of public values, not the argv refusals.
issues.suggested_fix: Do not use the ambient file and service names (PGSERVICE, PGSERVICEFILE, PGPASSFILE) as needles: drop them, but don't match on them. Give needles a minimum length (8, like the password needle). A shorter declared value is injected and named on the banner as 'not redacted (too short)', and doctor WARNs about it. Add tests for a 3-character declared value and an inherited PGSERVICE=dev.
issues.failure_scenario: The shell exports `PGSERVICE=dev`, and the supabase pack is declared. `npx cookwright run dev -- npm run dev` is refused with exit 125, 'argument 3 holds the value of PGSERVICE'. In the same way, a target declaring `STRIPE_MODE=test` refuses `-- npm test` and rewrites every 'test' in the output to `<STRIPE_MODE>`. It also drops an unrelated `NODE_ENV=test` from the child's environment.
issues.evidence: Disposition 68 and disposition 22: PGSERVICE/PGSERVICEFILE/PGPASSFILE are dropped but never needles, inherited values are needles only at 8+ characters (§6 'a short inherited value not a needle'); declared values stay needles by deliberate choice, documented in §11 and the guide ('a short or public declared value redacts its every occurrence'), with removed names shown on the banner.

issues.location: disposition 13 (200 ms drain, 'a grandchild that keeps the pipe open past that writes unseen')
issues.problem: After the child exits, the plan calls `end()` on the Redactor but says nothing about the pipe handles themselves. If they stay open and referenced, Node keeps reading and the process does not exit while a grandchild (a daemon or a `&` job) holds the write end. If they are destroyed instead, the grandchild's next write gets EPIPE or SIGPIPE and it dies. Either way 'writes unseen' is not what happens, and §6 does not test either case.
issues.suggested_fix: Choose and state one behaviour. For example, after 200 ms `unref()` the pipes and stop forwarding, so cookwright exits and a grandchild's writes go to a still-open but unread pipe until the buffer fills. Or say plainly that a grandchild dies on EPIPE. Test it with a child that runs `(sleep 1; echo x) &`.
issues.failure_scenario: `run dev -- sh -c 'some-server & exit 0'`. With the pipe still referenced, cookwright hangs until some-server exits, which blocks the agent's shell call until its timeout. With the pipe destroyed, some-server is killed by SIGPIPE on its first log line, contradicting the guide's 'writes unseen'.
issues.evidence: Disposition 59 chooses one behaviour: no 200 ms drain, run exits only after both pipes close, so a daemonising grandchild keeps run alive as a shell pipeline would; the guide names the in-command redirection (§4.7, §11); §6 tests a grandchild holding the pipe for a second.

issues.problem: `secrets.targets` runs git (`ls-files`, `check-ignore`, the diff against HEAD) but is registered with `config: true` only. probes.ignored and gitRun throw `probeFailed` when git cannot run, and runOne turns that into FAIL 'the check could not run', which breaks the 'never fails on absence' rule. Separately, the three rows sit before `repo.node_modules` (required at level 0, src/lib/levels.mjs:29) and `packs` in CHECKS order, and share the 1800 ms budget. Per-name `security` lookups across several keychain targets can therefore spend the budget, and the required row SKIPs.
issues.suggested_fix: Register `secrets.targets` with `config: true, git: true`. Place the three secrets rows after `packs`, at the end of CHECKS, so a slow backend cannot starve a required row. Alternatively, cap the keychain inspect's share of the budget, and add a doctor test showing that a spent budget inside inspect leaves `repo.node_modules` measured.
issues.failure_scenario: A keychain repo with two targets of six names makes twelve `security find-generic-password` calls at session start. They use up the shared budget, `repo.node_modules` SKIPs 'unverified: git ls-files', and the readout says 'level 0 declared: not verified' on a healthy repo. Separately, on a machine where git is not on PATH, `secrets.targets` FAILs instead of SKIP 'needs git'.
issues.evidence: Disposition 69 and §4.6: secrets.targets registered config: true, git: true; the three rows at the end of CHECKS after packs; §6 doctor test asserts a spent budget inside inspect leaves repo.node_modules measured.

issues.problem: SCANNED lists the top-level command files one by one (`src/init.mjs`, `src/doctor.mjs`, …). Disposition 35 adds only `src/lib/secrets` and `src/lib/secrets/backends`. The two new command modules, `src/run.mjs` and `src/secrets.mjs`, are not scanned, so prose literals there escape the 'user-facing strings in one place' test.
issues.suggested_fix: Add `src/run.mjs` and `src/secrets.mjs` to SCANNED in s1 or s2, alongside the directories.
issues.failure_scenario: s2 writes the banner's 'child output piped through the redactor' or a consent prompt as an inline literal in src/run.mjs or src/secrets.mjs. messages.test.mjs stays green, and the string never reaches the per-session strings batch the playbook escalates to the developer.
issues.evidence: Disposition 35 and §4.8: SCANNED gains src/run.mjs and src/secrets.mjs alongside src/lib/secrets and src/lib/secrets/backends.

issues.problem: The resolved output of `op inject` is parsed line by line at the first `=`. A 1Password field that holds a newline, which the plan defers to the backlog, is detected only when its continuation line is 'malformed'. A continuation line that itself looks like `NAME=value` parses as another assignment, and the plan does not say to check the parsed names against the template's refs.
issues.suggested_fix: Require the parsed output to have exactly as many lines as the template has refs, with the same names in the same order and no duplicates. Refuse otherwise, naming the line number only. Test with a field value of 'a\nDB_URL=x'.
issues.failure_scenario: SERVICE_ROLE_KEY's 1Password field holds a pasted .env snippet ending in a line 'DB_URL=postgresql://…prod…'. op inject outputs two lines for it, parseEnv yields a second DB_URL, and depending on map order the dev target injects prod's database URL. The template check never saw it, because the template only held refs.
issues.evidence: Disposition 53 and §4.3 onepassword.mjs parseAgainst(stdout, refs): exactly one line per template reference, same names in the same order, no other line; a multi-line field is refused as an extra line; §6 tests the LD_PRELOAD=x continuation and a wrong order.

issues.problem: age ciphertext carries no sender authentication. Anyone who can read the public `recipients.txt` can write a valid `secrets/<target>.env.age` holding values of their choosing. The recipients guard stops encryption to a new key, but nothing in the plan or the guide says that a ciphertext change from someone else cannot be reviewed and may hold attacker values. Doctor PASSes it as 'ciphertext and recipients tracked'.
issues.suggested_fix: Have the guide say that a change to `secrets/*.env.age` not made by the developer's own `secrets set` is unreviewable and is re-set rather than merged. Unproved names are the exposure. Log a signed-ciphertext or MAC enhancement in the backlog.
issues.failure_scenario: A contributor's PR replaces `secrets/dev.env.age` with a file encrypted to the committed recipients, keeping SUPABASE_URL and DB_URL so the proof still passes but changing the unproved SENTRY_DSN or a webhook URL to their own endpoint. The opaque diff is merged, doctor PASSes, and `run dev` injects the attacker's endpoint without a word.
issues.evidence: Disposition 70, §1, §4.7, §9: the guide says a secrets/*.env.age change not made by the developer's own secrets set is unreviewable (no sender authentication) and is re-set rather than merged, unproved names being the exposure; signed ciphertext is a backlog entry.
